title: Leadership Pursuing Pragmatic Leadership You Can't Check Your Ego at the Door
author: Pursuing Pragmatic Leadership
summary: The author reframes the ego not as an enemy to be eliminated but as a protection system that all humans carry -- one whose job is to keep us safe, accepted, respected, and in control. The conventional leadership advice to 'check your ego at the door' is argued to be unrealistic and counterproductive: the ego cannot be suppressed but merely goes underground, leaking out sideways through defensiveness, perfectionism, and validation-seeking -- often more destructively than an acknowledged ego. The healthier approach is ego awareness and regulation: getting curious about what the ego is trying to protect when it activates (usually fear of insignificance or inadequacy), working with it rather than declaring war on it. The article includes a personal narrative of the author catching their own ego activation in real time -- feeling a rising heartbeat during feedback -- and choosing curiosity over defensiveness. The conclusion is that real leadership is not ego elimination but ego integration: understanding oneself deeply enough that ambition can serve values rather than validate identity.
points: * The ego is not arrogance -- it is the protection system every human carries, wired to maintain safety, acceptance, respect, and control. The problem for leaders is not having an ego but letting it run the room unregulated. * Suppressing the ego doesn't work: a suppressed ego doesn't disappear -- it leaks out sideways in defensiveness, justification, control, perfectionism, and validation-seeking, often more destructively than an acknowledged ego. * Leaders who most loudly present as ego-less are sometimes the most controlled by it: their identity now depends on being perceived as humble or selfless -- the ego has simply morphed into protecting a different self-image. * The diagnostic question when ego activates is: Why am I reacting so strongly? Usually, underneath the ego's protective response is fear -- fear of being insignificant, fear of not being enough -- and naming that fear is the first step. * Real leadership is ego awareness and regulation, not ego elimination: the goal is to understand yourself so well that ambition and drive serve your values and purpose rather than constantly seeking to validate your identity.
quotes: Our ego isn't arrogance, or any other negatively labeled characteristic. It's our protection system -- the part of our wiring trying to keep us safe, accepted, respected, and in control.

When people say 'check your ego at the door,' what they really mean is don't let your ego drive your decisions and actions -- don't let it run the room. I agree with that. But it's not something we can hang up on the coat rack outside the room.

A suppressed ego doesn't disappear. It leaks out sideways, often in obnoxious and childish behaviors -- through defensiveness, justification, control, perfectionism, validation-seeking, and the inability to receive feedback.
So much of leadership dysfunction comes from leaders pretending to 'keep their ego in check' while being subconsciously driven by it.

The irony is that leaders who try hardest to appear ego-less are sometimes the most controlled by it. Because now their identity depends on being perceived as humble, evolved, or selfless. The ego just morphed into protecting something else.

Usually, underneath the ego is fear. Fear of being insignificant. Fear of not being enough. It is our internal identity and sense of self-worth, and when we understand that, we stop treating the ego like an enemy and start treating it like information.
Real leadership isn't ego elimination. It's ego awareness and understanding to enable regulation, and knowing who we are without the need to prove anything.
